extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in classical geometry and the quadrature of the circle
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric constructions and diagrammatic demonstrations relating areas, perimeters, diameters and circumferences of circles, squares, rectangles, regular polygons, and right-angled triangles; includes numeric examples and mean-proportional relations used to argue equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perimeter-of-isosceles equals circumference (4/5 rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sides of an isosceles triangle be equal to twice the base, the perimeter of the triangle is equal to the circumference of a circle, of which the diameter is equal to four-fifths of the side of the triangle, or eight-fifths of its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (diagram No.12 / Fig. XXI): with sides D L and D B = 10 and base L B = 5, perimeter 10+10+5 = 25 equals the circumference of generating circle X (constructed so its circumference is 25 when AB = 8). The same construction yields a second equal isosceles triangle whose perimeter likewise equals the same circumference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle with long side = 2 x short side equals circle area (4/5 diameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a rectangle, of which the value of the longer sides is equal to twice the value of the shorter sides, is equal in area to the area of a circle, of which the diameter is equal to four-fifths of the longer sides, or eight-fifths of the shorter sides of the rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (diagram No.12): rectangles D B G N and D B H P have longer side 10 and shorter side 5, so area 10 x 5 = 50, which equals the area of the generating circle X (constructed with AB = 8 giving circle area 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangles from isosceles construction equal generating circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectangles formed by taking segments at right angles to the diameter and paralleling the extended diameter (DBGN, DBHP) have area equal to the generating circle X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed so GB = BH = 5 and GN = HP = 10, each rectangle area 50 = area of circle X in the given numeric example (AB = 8, circumference 25, circle area 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribed square equals twice generating circle; inscribed circle and inscribed square relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The square NGHP constructed has area equal to twice the area of generating circle X; a circle Y inscribed in NGHP and a square RSTV inscribed in Y have areas tied to circle X (RSTV area equals area of circle X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With NGHP side 10, area 100 = 2 x area(circle X) = 2 x 50. Inscribed circle Y then has area (author's numeric datum) 78.125 and the inscribed square RSTV in Y has area 50, equal to area(circle X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius equals hexagon side — mapping to regular hexagon
rubrics_metrics.description: The radius of the inscribed circle Y equals the side of a regular hexagon inscribed in Y, so the base L B (and M B) of the isosceles triangles equals the side of that regular hexagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because C B (radius of circle Y) = L B = 5 in the example, L B and M B may be interpreted as the side of an inscribed regular hexagon; the author notes one may deform the quadrilateral perimeter into an inscribed regular hexagon touching the circumference at six equidistant points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle area as mean proportional between square-on-diameter and semicircle area
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of the generating circle X is the mean proportional between the area of a square described on its diameter and the area of the semi-circle G C H (or either semi-circle into which circle Y is divided by the diameter DB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric example: diameter of X = 8, square on diameter area 64; semi-circle GCH area = 9.0625; sqrt(64 x 9.0625) = 50 = area(circle X). The author generalizes that similar computations hold for other hypothetical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every square inscribed in a circle is mean proportional between circumscribed square and square on radius
rubrics_metrics.description: If a square is inscribed in any circle, the area of such square is the mean proportional between the area of a square circumscribed about the circle and the area of a square described on a radius of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for circle X with circumscribed square area 400 and square on radius area 100, sqrt(400 x 100) = 200 which equals the area of the inscribed square. The statement is given in several numeric instances showing the mean-proportional property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every circle is mean proportional between certain squares
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of every circle is a mean proportional between the area of a square circumscribed about it, or described on its diameter, and the area of a square of which the perimeter is equal to the circumference of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author demonstrates with hypothetical data (both his own datum and the 'orthodox' π ≈ 3.1416 values) that the area of a circle can be expressed as the geometric mean of two appropriately chosen square areas (e.g., circumscribed square and square whose perimeter equals the circle's circumference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric mean relations in series of circles (doubling areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a succession of circles each containing twice the area of the preceding one, pick any three adjacent circles c, d, e: the middle circle d has area equal to the mean proportional between areas of e and c; the same mean-proportional relation holds for diameters and circumferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: take areas 16 (c), 32 (d), 64 (e): sqrt(16 x 64) = 32. The author similarly shows sqrt(circumference_c x circumference_e) = circumference_d and sqrt(diameter_c x diameter_e) = diameter_d in his numeric construction (diagram No.14 / Fig. XXIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-triangle (3:4 ratio) construction yields commensurable 3-4-5 triangle and Pythagorean-area grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: If on AB describe a right-angled triangle ABC with BC equal to three-fourths of AB, then ABC is a 3-4-5 triangle (if AB=4, BC=3, AC=5) and the areas of squares on sides AB and BC together equal the area of the square on AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author shows with AB=4 that AB^2 + BC^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 = AC^2, and generalizes that if the two sides adjacent to the right angle are in ratio 3:4, the middle side is the arithmetic mean of the other two in his symbolic arithmetic framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle X equals square AC H I (Pythagorean equality) and equals square + trapezium decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of circle X (in the true-theory numerics used by the author) equals the area of square A C H I (25 in the example) and is also equal to the sum of the area of square A K L B and the trapezium A R L T A in the diagram (i.e., circle X = square AKLB + trapezium ARLTA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for AB=4 and the author's area datum, square AC H I area 25 equals area(circle X). The author demonstrates that square AKLB (16) + trapezium ARLTA (9) = 25, which equals area(circle X). He contrasts these equalities when orthodox π-based values are used, showing numerical discrepancies in that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple groupings of three figures have equal total area equal to a larger circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the diagrams there are distinct sets of three geometric figures whose areas together equal the area of a larger circumscribed circle (circle Y); examples include various combinations of circles, squares, and trapeziums listed by the author that sum to the same total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author enumerates many instances: e.g., circle X + square AKLB + trapezium ARLTA = 25 + 16 + 9 = 50 = area(circle Y) (in his datum); similarly square AC H I + square A B F G + square B D E C = 25 + 16 + 9 = 50, and other permutations — and contrasts these with the orthodox numerical data where the equalities fail.
